routes.description: Establish historical credibility for bodily resurrection and Catholic continuity through early Pauline testimony, substantively stable textual transmission, external identification of early Christian belief, and persistence of apostolic church structures and doctrines.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Paul warrants a bodily-resurrection reading, transmission and hostile-witness evidence reliably identify early Christian belief, and institutional and doctrinal continuities connect the first-century church with later Catholic and related apostolic communions.

motionBridge.description: Connect the Pauline, transmission, hostile-witness, and church-structure evidence to the historical credibility of bodily resurrection and Catholic continuity.

centralBridges.description: Establish that the early undisputed Pauline letters attest a real bodily resurrection and a risen-Christ appearance rather than merely an immaterial vision.
Establish that manuscript stability and external testimony preserve and independently identify an early, historically rooted Christian belief tradition.
Trace first-century leadership offices and essential doctrines through the pre-Nicene period and later apostolic communions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show that Roman, Eastern Orthodox, and Syriac differences coexist with substantial agreement on essential doctrines, councils, and apostolic orders.
Distinguish reforms that retained inherited Catholic doctrine from later movements that discarded it when characterizing historical continuity.

routes.description: Deny that the cited materials establish bodily resurrection or a uniquely Catholic lineage by emphasizing visionary and secondhand alternatives for Paul, uncertainty in transmission and preservation, early Christian diversity, and context-dependent religious branching.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Pauline reports remain compatible with visionary or inherited interpretations, surviving sources cannot securely overcome transmission and selection uncertainty, or early diversity and later branching prevent identification of one continuous Catholic institution.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined evidence named in the motion remains insufficient to make bodily resurrection and Catholic continuity historically credible.

centralBridges.description: Show that Paul's experience and witness traditions do not establish a bodily encounter or independently prove an earlier resurrection event.
Show that copying gaps, oral and written transmission, authorial selection, and selective survival limit the evidential force of Christian and hostile sources.
Show that competing early groups, divergent regional churches, and conciliar formation complicate identification of a uniquely continuous Catholic orthodoxy.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require the continuity case to distinguish the existence of a small pre-Constantinian group from widespread or uniquely authoritative orthodoxy.
Use earlier reform movements and shared Christian scripture and history to test claims that later divisions constitute categorical religious rupture.

sections.title: Pauline evidence and bodily resurrection
sections.rationale: The earliest Pauline material is central to whether the resurrection claim concerns a tangible risen body and whether Paul's reported experience and inherited witness list provide independent historical support.

sections.title: Textual stability and Gospel transmission
sections.rationale: Historical use of Christian writings depends on distinguishing substantive manuscript stability from uncertainty about earlier sources, interpolations, transmission across decades, and authorial selection.

sections.title: Hostile witnesses and preservation effects
sections.rationale: External descriptions may help identify early Christian beliefs, but their force depends on whether surviving hostile materials independently represent the period or reflect selective preservation.

sections.title: Early orthodoxy and institutional continuity
sections.rationale: The Catholic-continuity burden turns on whether first-century leadership structures persist through the pre-Nicene era despite a small population, competing groups, councils, and uncertainty about early development.

sections.title: Apostolic communions, reform, and religious branching
sections.rationale: Comparisons among Catholic, Orthodox, Syriac, and Protestant traditions test whether shared doctrine, councils, orders, scripture, and history demonstrate continuity or instead support multiple context-dependent Christian branches.
